title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC), model-serving, observability, and performance. It includes operational guardrails and the format/process for Architectural Decision Records (ADRs). The intent is to provide a single, opinionated reference teams can follow to ensure consistency, reliability, and measurable service-level outcomes across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope

- Applies to all services that participate in the Redwood inference platform (hosted API, dedicated, private).
- Primary audience: service owners, platform engineers, runtime team, SDK/docs engineers, SRE.
- Exceptions require an ADR and approval from the architecture review board (see ADR process).

Principles

1. Developer-first, production-oriented: prioritize clear APIs, reliable defaults, measurable SLOs, and simple onboarding.
2. Observable by default: every service must emit standard metrics, traces, and structured logs.
3. Failure-resilient: graceful degradation, fallbacks, and circuit-breakers for external dependencies.
4. Cost-aware: designs should consider unit economics (tokens/second, batch sizing, KV cache reuse).
5. Automate and document runbooks and rollbacks for all production changes.

1) API Standards

Summary: All externally-facing and internal RPC/REST APIs should be designed for clarity, versionability, and forward/backward compatibility. Prefer small, composable endpoints over large RPC surfaces.

Requirements:
- Protocols: REST+JSON for public HTTP APIs; gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs.
- Base path and naming: use kebab-case for paths (e.g., /v1/generate, /v1/embeddings), plural resources when modeling collections.
- Versioning: Major version in path (/v1/). Non-breaking changes use content negotiation or new optional fields. Breaking changes require a documented migration path and >= 90 days deprecation.
- Authentication: bearer tokens (OAuth2/JWT) for public APIs; MTLS for service-to-service where sensitive data is involved. Secrets via KMS-integrated vaults (see infra standards).
- Error model: RFC 7807 Problem Details JSON for errors. Include machine-readable error_code and human_message. Provide a stable set of error_codes in API docs.
- Rate limiting & quotas: include per-API headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset). Default throttle policy for new endpoints:  R=500 requests/min per token (adjust per-product via feature flags).
- Pagination: cursor-based (opaque cursors) for lists.
- Streaming: server-sent events (SSE) for hosted generation streaming endpoints; fallback to chunked transfer for compatibility.

Example (HTTP request/response):

Request:
POST /v1/generate
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "model": "redwood-1-small",
  "input": "Summarize the following..."
}

Error response (problem details):
{
  "type": "https://api.redwood.ai/errors/insufficient_quota",
  "title": "Insufficient quota",
  "status": 403,
  "error_code": "QUOTA_EXCEEDED",
  "human_message": "Your organization has exceeded the monthly token quota. Contact billing."
}

2) Coding Standards

Languages and ownership:
- Service languages: Go for core platform services (router-service, runtime-gateway); Python for model inference helpers and evals; TypeScript for web/console frontends and SDKs.
- Critical runtime code must be instrumented and peer-reviewed by an owner on the runtime team.

Style and tooling:
- Use linters and formatters as gate checks (golangci-lint for Go, black/isort + flake8 for Python, eslint + prettier for TypeScript).
- Must include typed public interfaces for libraries (Go interfaces/TypeScript types).
- Unit test coverage: minimum 60% for business logic; 80%+ for core infra logic. Use mutation testing selectively for critical paths.
- Dependency policy: minimal direct dependencies in runtime path. All third-party libs must be approved via dependency-review pipeline.

Code review and CI:
1. All changes require PR review from at least 2 engineers (one from owning team).
2. CI must run linters, unit tests, integration smoke tests, and an SCA scan.
3. Merge gating: green CI + approver + successful canary plan in feature flag system for runtime changes.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC / Cloud / Networking)

IaC and repo layout:
- Terraform for cloud infra (module per top-level service). Reuse central modules in //infra/modules.
- Environment separation: account per environment (prod, staging, dev) with cross-account trust where needed.
- Naming convention: {env}-{service}-{component}-{region} (e.g., prod-router-usw2).

Networking and security:
- VPC peering or Transit Gateway for private deployments; default deny security groups; explicit allow for management ports only.
- Subnets: separate control plane vs data plane subnets for private/Dedicated deployments.
- Secrets: use customer-managed KMS for private; KMS + Vault for hosted; no secrets in plain Terraform state (state in encrypted S3 + DynamoDB).

Capacity and autoscaling:
- Autoscaling policies defined with target utilization (e.g., 60% GPU memory utilization, 70% GPU compute utilization) and cooldown windows documented in module variables.
- Quota guardrails: soft- and hard- limits configured per account; alerting when soft limits exceed 80%.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Goals: predictable latency, reproducible models, safe rollouts, and measurable quality regressions.

Packaging and artifacts:
- Models must be published as immutable artifacts in the model registry with semantic-version metadata (model_name:version+quantization). Include: git-hash, training-dataset-tag, tokenizer-version, quantization-profile, expected VRAM.
- Acceptable artifact formats: TorchScript, ONNX (runtime-validated), or Redwood-compiled bundle. Provide compatibility matrix in model registry.

Inference configuration:
- Default KV caching: enabled for autoregressive models; eviction policy LRU with TTL default 24h for hosted caches.
- Batching: runtime should support dynamic batching. Default batch targets: 8 (latency-sensitive), 64 (throughput-optimized) depending on policy. Max batch size must be validated per model via benchmarking job.
- Quantization profiles: maintain profiles per model and hardware class (fp16, int8, q4_0). Include expected accuracy delta <= 1.5% for recommended quantization.

Rollout & fallback:
1. Canary: 1-5% traffic for 24-48 hours with automatic quality regression checks (see Evals).
2. Monitor latency, error rate, and quality. If any of: latency p95 increases by >20%, error rate >1% absolute, or eval metric regression >2% relative, auto-fallback to previous version.
3. Manual rollback: documented runbook in runtime runbooks directory.

Model safety and privacy:
- Models that handle PII must have data-flow diagrams and a privacy review.
- For Private deployments, keys and data residency must match customer contract.

5) Observability Standards

Metric conventions (prometheus labels):
- Required labels: service, environment, region, model (if applicable), route, team.
- Counters: requests_total{status="200|4xx|5xx"}, tokens_consumed_total, cache_hits_total, cache_misses_total.
- Histograms: request_latency_seconds_bucket (le=0.01,0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2,5).

Logs:
- Structured JSON logs at INFO/ERROR levels. Include request_id, trace_id, user_org_id (when applicable), model_version, route. No PII in logs.

Tracing:
- OpenTelemetry first-class. Span naming: <service>.<operation> (e.g., runtime.forward, router.route). Sample rate: 10% by default; increase to 100% for post-incident capture windows.

Dashboards & alerts:
- Per-route latency and error dashboards for top 20 routes.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - High error rate: error rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m -> P1 pager.
  - Latency SLO breach: p95 latency > SLO by 20% for 10m -> P1.
  - Cache eviction storm: cache_misses_total increase > 200% over baseline for 5m -> P2.

SLO template (apply per service/route):
- Objective: 99.9% availability (success rate) per week.
- Latency: p50, p95, p99 targets defined per route (examples below).
- Error budget and burn rate policies documented in eng-sre/runbooks.

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarks

Latency SLO examples (hosted text generation, short prompt workload):
- p50 < 50 ms (token emission path; note: depends heavily on model & hardware).
- p95 < 300 ms.
- p99 < 800 ms.
- Tail targets for cold-cache model load: p99 < 3s for first-request warmup.

Throughput targets and GPU guidance:
- Baseline small model (redwood-1-small) on A100: ~120 tokens/sec per GPU for token-generation baseline with batch sizing 16.
- Medium model (redwood-1-medium) on A100: ~50-80 tokens/sec per GPU.
- Batching guidance: prefer dynamic batching with latency-aware maximums. When latency SLO is strict (e.g., p95 < 300ms), cap batch sizes to limit queuing delay (recommend target batch <= 8).

Benchmarking suite:
- All model onboarding must include a standardized benchmark run (see eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite). Benchmarks must exercise common prompt lengths (16, 64, 256 tokens) and measure latency distribution, memory usage, and failure modes.

7) Architectural Decision Records (ADRs)

Purpose: capture design context, alternatives, and decisions that materially affect cross-team architecture. ADRs are required for changes that:
- Introduce or replace core infra (new runtime scheduler, serialization format change, major API breaking change).
- Affect customer contracts (data residency, SLA changes).

ADRs format (single-file markdown stored in architecture repo):
- Title: short descriptive title
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded
- Context: why is decision needed
- Decision: what we decided and why
- Consequences: operational impacts, rollout plan, migration steps, owners
- Date and related PRs/links

ADRs process:
1. Author creates ADR draft and notifies architecture review board (ARB).
2. 7-day review window (shorter for emergencies). Reviewers: ARB + affected teams.
3. Approval: 2 approvals including at least one architecture owner.
4. Publish: Accepted ADR added to confluence + archived in git repo with tags.

Example ADRs (referencing current decisions):
- ADR-2025-07: Standardize on gRPC for internal control plane RPCs (accepted).
- ADR-2025-11: Adopt Problem Details JSON for API errors (accepted).
- ADR-2026-02: Default KV cache TTL and LRU eviction for hosted caches (accepted).

8) Ownership, Change Control & Enforcement

- Each top-level standard area has a documented owner and on-call:
  - API standards: API guild lead (owner: Daniel Kim)
  - Runtime/Model-serving: Runtime team (owner: Aisha Patel)
  - Observability: SRE team (owner: Maria Gomez)
  - Infra/IaC: Cloud infra team (owner: Rajesh Singh)

- Enforcement: PR templates include a standards checklist. Random quarterly audits by architecture team. Non-compliant changes must create ADRs or include a mitigation plan.

9) Rollout checklist for breaking changes (services/runtime/infra)

1. Draft ADR and obtain ARB approval.
2. Update docs & developer quickstart.
3. Add feature flags and canary routing rule (1-5% traffic).
4. Run integration tests and performance benchmark in staging.
5. Deploy canary and monitor for 24-48h: latency, errors, eval metrics.
6. Gradual traffic ramp (5% -> 25% -> 100%) only after green checks at each step.
7. Execute rollback plan on any automatic failure case.

Appendix A - Key config table

- default-batching-target: "8|64" (string list; use policy per route)
- cache-ttl-default: "24h"
- canary-duration: "24-48h"
- api-rate-limit-default: "500/min/token"
- slo-availability-weekly: "99.9%"

Document maintenance

- Owners must review this page quarterly and update ADR references as new accepted decisions are published.
- For urgent changes (security/perf incidents), an emergency ADR cadence is allowed with shortened review.

Contact

For questions or exceptions, contact the architecture review board (architecture@redwood.ai) or the owners listed above.
